Review record · M6 stage 2 · item 2 of review/2026-09-14-m6s2-rule · evidence 2026-10-25 · repository at f1dc820

The deck reading, walked through

Your call

What you are deciding, and why it matters

Your rule of 2026-09-14 reads: “if it would compile in 1962, it should compile. If it wouldn't, it shouldn't. If it's ambiguous, I need to see it with argumentation both ways and a recommendation, and I'll make a call.” The 1960 payroll program, keyed exactly as printed, is the case that splits the word “compile”. Under the 1962 manual's own rules the processor would have printed a full listing of 55 messages, and punched an object deck, and refused to run it. We can reproduce the listing to the byte. No evidence describes what was on the deck. So: does “it should compile” mean we must print the listing, or that we must also punch that deck? The answer fixes how two refusals in the compiler are labelled, and whether we may ever write code that no evidence describes.

The 30-second version

  1. The 1962 processor never saw this deck. Every step below is what J's letter says it would have done. Nothing here is a record of a run in 1962.
  2. Our compiler reads the 191 cards and prints the listing: 55 messages of 12 kinds, highest code 4, and SEVERITY LIMIT WAS NOT REACHED.
  3. J's rule: only a code of 5 stops the deck (J 02.01.01). Any code above 1 stops the run (J 90.04.02). So, under our severity table, J punches a deck and does not run it. No 1962 severity value survives (J 90.04.01): the 4 is our choice (D7.5).
  4. Our generator stops at the first GET, statement 3,00, with a GET record on 0 input files (no sample instance). It punches an empty deck: a 12-byte header and no cards.
  5. Recommendation: option 1, the listing. Keep the refusal and relabel it “1962 punched a deck whose content no evidence describes”. The other options must invent code (against D0.4) or invent a severity.
  6. New since 2026-09-15: the FILE-IN decision of 2026-10-24 added a second refusal of the same kind (messages 195,00 and 22,00, our severity 3). The design record says your answer decides both. No work is blocked.

Provenance. Item 2 of the record on branch review/2026-09-14-m6s2-rule (tip ef57893) asked this question. On 2026-09-15 you answered the other items and kept item 2 open: its banner records that you asked for a walkthrough of the deck reading before you decide. This record is that walkthrough. It re-argues nothing that record decided. Every repository path below is at commit f1dc820 (master, 2026-10-25). Every run output below is captured in evidence/, not retyped.

Citation forms. J 02.01.01 cites J28-6169 (1962) by IBM section code; F p. 101 cites F28-8043 (1960) by printed page. D0.4 is a locked decision; M6-9 an entry in docs/design/m6-acceptance.md. 108,00 is a message number; 5,01 in a listing is a statement number. inferred marks a claim that no source states.

SEVERITY LIMIT WAS NOT REACHED

    None of the twelve messages is worded as a stop, a deletion or a repair. J has that vocabulary and uses it elsewhere: 2,00 “-RUN- DELETED.”, 171,00 “SENTENCE DELETED FROM TEXT.” (J 90.04.01). The compiler completes, as J 05.06.01 says it does “unless a catastrophic error occurs”.

    The severity gate

    Three passages decide what happens after the listing. First, what the codes mean:

    Second, the deck. Only a 5 suppresses it:

    So, under our table, J's letter punches a deck and does not run it. That conclusion is only as firm as the 4. If any one of the twelve kinds carried a 5 in 1962, no deck was punched. No evidence settles that.

    Two smaller points. Our control card asks for LIST only, not LOAD, so it asks for no run in any case; the card is our reconstruction (D7.12). And J 02.01.02's “undefined symbol in the code which it has generated” is a bar on generated code. Message 108,00 reports an undefined name in the source. Whether the 26 source names became undefined generated symbols is not stated. inferred

    Open Question 66 already asks the next question: “Does a severity 2–4 error make the punched object deck unreliable, or merely suppress automatic execution?” (docs/comtran-language-definition.md).

    Step 4 of 6

    What the deck would hold

    What we know

    Step 5 of 6

    Your call

    The fork

    Two readings of “it should compile”. Each is a fair reading of your rule.

    Compile = the listing

    Option 1 · recommended

    What it says
    To compile is to read the deck and print the listing. Under J's letter 1962 would have done that, and we do it, to the byte.
    What the compiler must do
    Nothing new. Keep the refusal. Relabel it: “1962 punched a deck whose content no evidence describes”, not “1962 refused”.
    What it must invent
    Nothing.
    What breaks
    Nothing.
    Left unbuilt
    The object form of a program that could never run.
    What a later reader is misled about
    Nothing, once the label is fixed. Today's label is the one thing that misleads.
    Cost to reverse
    One edit to M6-9 and one to the corpus test's comment (the 2026-09-14 record's costing), plus the refusal class comment on our reading of step 4.

    Compile = the object deck

    What it says
    To compile in 1962 was to punch a deck. J 02.01.01 ties the deck to the severity code alone. A compiler that stops short of the deck has not compiled.

    Option 2 · build the deck

    What the compiler must do
    Generate code for every site of step 4: GET and FILE on records with no file, FILE IN a name that is no file, 26 undefined names, an empty GRAND.TOTAL.
    What it must invent, against which decision
    All of it. D0.4: where no evidence survives, behaviour is “a recorded design decision … never presented as historical fact”. Here there is not even a shape to record.
    What a later reader is misled about
    The deck would look like a recovery and would be a guess.
    Cost to reverse
    Delete that code and its golden.

    Option 3 · rule a severity of 5

    What the compiler must do
    Raise one of the twelve kinds to 5. Then J stops the compile, no deck is due, and the refusal is right for the right reason.
    What it must invent, against which decision
    The 5. J 90.04.01 prints 0 for every message (Open Question 65). D7.5 documents the table “as a recorded design decision, never as recovered historical fact”.
    What a later reader is misled about
    A severity that reads as recovered and was chosen. The listing would also change: it would close SEVERITY LIMIT WAS REACHED, a wording that is itself our decision (D7.6).
    Cost to reverse
    One row of the severity table and one golden rebuild.
    Recommendation

    Option 1. M6-9: “Keep the refusal for the verbatim deck, and relabel it. The honest label is ‘1962 punched a deck whose content no evidence describes’, not ‘1962 refused’. Take the listing as the deliverable of that deck.” The reason: it is the only option that states what the evidence supports and invents nothing. The deck is real under J's letter; its content is not recoverable, and saying so is the finding.
